title: David Gans, a student of the Maharal, observed the stars with Tycho Brahe and Kepler and wrote the chronicle "Tzemach David"

trailer.text: David Gans (1541–1613) was a Jewish historian and astronomer who wrote works on history and the sciences in Hebrew.
According to an article by Noah Efron, David Gans was a German Jew who was educated in Poland and spent his adulthood in Prague.
He was one of the students of the Maharal, and despite his rabbinical education he was drawn to Renaissance culture, according to the National Library of Israel blog.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, his book Tzemach David was published in Prague in 1592, a chronicle in two parts: the annals of Jewish history and general history.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, in Prague he came into contact with Kepler and Tycho Brahe and took part in astronomical observations at the observatory.
He described in Hebrew what he saw and learned in their company in the book Nechmad ve-Naim, according to the National Library of Israel blog.

paragraphs.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, David Gans was born in 1541 in Lippstadt, Westphalia.
He went to Cracow and studied there under Moses Isserles, the Rema.
Later he attended the lectures of the brothers, Löwe ben Bezalel of Prague and R. Sinai, according to the Jewish Encyclopedia.

According to the same source, the brothers introduced philosophy, mathematics and astronomy into the circle of their studies, and from them Gans received the impulse to devote himself to these sciences.
According to Mosaic Magazine, Gans also studied humanistic and scientific texts.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, he began writing studies on history and the sciences in Hebrew.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Gans settled in Prague in about 1564.

According to the National Library of Israel blog, around 1599, in the days of Emperor Rudolf II, who had moved his court from Vienna to Prague, Prague was an oasis of tolerance in an empire torn by religious tensions.
The city's Hebrew printing house, one of the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe, made it a center of Hebrew learning.
According to Google Arts & Culture, Gans was a contemporary of the Maharal and Mordecai Maisel.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, the crowding and plagues in the Jewish Quarter led him to leave Prague, but he continued his studies diligently.

stations.title: "Tzemach David": the history of Israel and the history of the world

paragraphs.text: According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Tzemach David was first published in Prague in 1592.
According to Google Arts & Culture, the first part briefly recounts Jewish history from the Creation to 1592.
The second part deals with the history of the then known world and covers the same period.
According to Google Arts & Culture, Gans used not only Hebrew sources but also non-Jewish chronicles.
According to Kikar HaShabbat, at the beginning of the second part he apologizes for the book having been compiled from non-Jewish sources.
According to the same source, he emphasized that he had translated many gentile books dealing with history.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Gans tried to show in the preface that it was permitted to read history on the Sabbath.
According to Kikar HaShabbat, he wrote that there are sages who hold that his book should not be read on the Sabbath, and brought proof for his position from his teacher, the Rema.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the book is memorable as the first work of its kind among the German Jews, who at that time appreciated historical knowledge but slightly.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, Tycho Brahe, the Danish astronomer and nobleman, arrived in Prague in 1599.
Brahe moved his observatory and research center to the "New Venice" castle north of Prague, not far from the village where Gans lived.
According to Mosaic Magazine, when Gans heard that Brahe was living at an imperial castle outside Prague, he seized the opportunity to meet him.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, Gans was self-taught, with no formal scientific education.
According to the same source, he received a warm welcome and learned from the best minds of his time.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Brahe charged Gans with translating the Alphonsine Tables from Hebrew into German.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, Gans contributed by translating Hebrew astronomical texts that were not available to Brahe and Kepler.

stations.title: "Nechmad ve-Naim": what he saw at the observatory

paragraphs.text: According to the National Library of Israel blog, in the book Nechmad ve-Naim Gans described in Hebrew his meeting with the two scientists and what he saw and learned in their company.
He describes in detail the observatory and Brahe's working methods there.
According to the same source, Gans wrote in the book that the use of astronomy to foretell the future is misguided.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the book deals with astronomy and mathematical geography and is divided into 12 chapters and 305 paragraphs.
It was published with additions by Joel ben Jekuthiel of Glogau, at Jessnitz in 1743.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Gans was acquainted with the work of Copernicus but followed the Ptolemaic system and attributed the Copernican system to the Pythagoreans.
According to the University of Rostock, Brahe regarded the earth as the center around which the sun revolves, and Kepler supported the system in which the sun is at the center.
According to the same source, the two astronomers were unable to agree on a common world model.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, Brahe died and was buried in the Church of Our Lady before Týn in the Old Town of Prague.
According to the University of Rostock, his sudden death cut short his project of planetary position tables, and the work was finally completed by Kepler.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, Kepler moved to Prague for a few years and served there as a scientist at the emperor's court.
Kepler and Gans corresponded, apparently in German mixed with Hebrew.
According to Efron, Gans believed that the sciences he described could mediate between Christians and Jews, as a shared subject of study.
According to Efron, Gans intimated that this belief was also shared by Kepler and Brahe.
According to the National Library of Israel blog, in 1613, the year in which David Gans died, Kepler left Prague in order to continue his research.
According to the Linda Hall Library, Tycho Brahe died on October 24, 1601.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, the first part of Tzemach David and extracts from the second were translated into Latin by Wilhelm Heinrich Vorst, in Leyden in 1644.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Tzemach David was also translated into Judæo-German by Solomon Hanau (Frankfort, 1692).
According to the National Library of Israel blog, Gans's book Nechmad VeNa'im can be read today in the original Hebrew on the National Library of Israel website.
According to the Jewish Encyclopedia, Gans's annals are very dry and have no great intrinsic value.
According to Kikar HaShabbat, the Yaavetz forbade regular study of the second part of "Tzemach David".
According to Efron, Gans's hopes were not fulfilled, and most of his books were not published and remained without attention.

disagreements.question: For how long, and in what way, was Gans in Brahe's company?

versions.says: Jewish Encyclopedia: took part in observations for three consecutive days
National Library of Israel blog: stayed at the castle for three weeks, likely excluding Fridays and Saturdays
Kikar HaShabbat: worked for his living at Brahe's observatory, together with Kepler

disagreements.question: Where did the observations take place?

versions.says: Jewish Encyclopedia: at the Prague observatory
National Library of Israel blog: at the "New Venice" castle north of Prague

unknowns.text: The exact year in which Gans visited Brahe: according to the National Library of Israel blog, Brahe arrived in Prague in 1599 and died about a year after the meeting with Gans, but the blog does not state the year of the visit.

claims.text: לפי מאמרו של נח אפרון (1997), דוד גנס (1541-1613) היה יהודי גרמני שלמד בפולין וחי את בגרותו בפראג, וכתב לאורך חייו קורפוס גדול וחסר תקדים של מבואות עבריים לתחומי מדע, בעיקר אסטרונומיה.
claims.quote: David Gans (1541-1613), a German Jew who was educated in Poland and spent his adulthood in Prague, produced over his lifetime a large and unprecedented corpus of Hebrew introductions

claims.text: לפי הבלוג של הספרייה הלאומית, גנס היה מתלמידי המהר"ל, ולמרות השכלתו הרבנית נמשך לתרבות הרנסנס והחל לכתוב בעברית מחקרים בהיסטוריה ובמדעים.
claims.quote: who despite his rabbinical education, was drawn to Renaissance culture and began writing studies on history and the sciences in Hebrew.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, "צמח דוד" פורסם לראשונה בפראג ב-1592 ומחולק לשני חלקים: הראשון עוסק בדברי ימי ישראל והשני בהיסטוריה הכללית.
claims.quote: published first at Prague, in 1592. It is divided into two parts, the first containing the annals of Jewish history, the second those of general history.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, גנס השתקע בפראג בסביבות 1564, בא שם במגע עם קפלר וטיכו ברהה, והשתתף שלושה ימים רצופים בתצפיות אסטרונומיות במצפה הכוכבים של פראג.
claims.quote: about 1564 settled at Prague. There he came into contact with Kepler and Tycho Brahe, and took part for three consecutive days in astronomical observations at the Prague observatory.

claims.text: לפי הבלוג של הספרייה הלאומית, גנס כתב בעברית את הספר "נחמד ונעים", המתאר את פגישתו עם שני המדענים הגדולים ואת מה שראה ולמד בחברתם.
claims.quote: in which he recounts his meeting with the two great scientists and what he saw and learned while he was in their company.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, דוד גנס היה היסטוריון ואסטרונום גרמני, שנולד בליפשטדט שבווסטפאליה ב-1541 ונפטר בפראג ב-25 באוגוסט 1613.
claims.quote: German historian; astronomer; born at Lippstadt, Westphalia, 1541; died at Prague Aug. 25, 1613.

claims.text: לפי גוגל ארטס ותרבות, דוד בן שלמה גנס נולד ב-1541 בליפשטדט שבגרמניה ונפטר ב-1613 בפראג.
claims.quote: David ben Salomon Gans (1541 Lippstadt, Germany - 1613 Prague, Czech Republic)

claims.text: לפי הנרי אברמסון, גנס (1541-1613) היה תלמיד של משה איסרלס והמהר"ל מפראג, שיתף פעולה באופן פעיל עם טיכו ברהה ויוהאנס קפלר והותיר חיבורים מלומדים חשובים.
claims.quote: A student of Rabbi Moshe Isserles and the Maharal of Prague, he collaborated actively with Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler and left behind important scholarly works.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, ספרו של גנס "נחמד ונעים", העוסק באסטרונומיה ובגאוגרפיה מתמטית, פורסם עם תוספות של יואל בן יקותיאל מגלוגוב ביסניץ ב-1743.
claims.quote: dealing with astronomy and mathematical geography, published with additions by Joel ben Jekuthiel of Glogau at Jessnitz, 1743.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, גנס נסע לקרקוב ולמד שם אצל משה איסרלס.
claims.quote: he went to Cracow, where he studied under Moses Isserles

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, גנס השתתף מאוחר יותר בשיעוריהם של האחים לֶוֶה בן בצלאל מפראג ושל ר' סיני.
claims.quote: Later he attended the lectures of the brothers Löwe ben Bezalel of Prague and of R. Sinai.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, האחים הכניסו פילוסופיה, מתמטיקה ואסטרונומיה למעגל לימודיהם, ומהם קיבל גנס את הדחף להתמסר לענפי מדע אלה.
claims.quote: They introduced philosophy, mathematics, and astronomy into the circle of their studies, and from them Gans received the impulse to devote himself to these branches of science.

claims.text: לפי מגזין מוסף (2021), גנס היה תלמידו של המהר"ל מפראג, למד גם טקסטים הומניסטיים ומדעיים וחיבר יצירה פורצת דרך בהיסטוריה יהודית.
claims.quote: A disciple of the famed Prague rabbi Judah Loew ben Betzalel (better known as the Maharal), he also studied humanistic and scientific texts, and authored a groundbreaking work on Jewish history.

claims.quote: Its Hebrew printing house, which was one of the first of its kind in Central and Eastern Europe, had transformed Prague into a center of Hebrew learning.

claims.text: לפי גוגל ארטס ותרבות, גנס, בן דורם של המהר"ל ומרדכי מייזל, קיים קשר הדוק עם מלומדים נוצרים כמו טיכו ברהה ויוהאנס קפלר.

claims.text: לפי אפרון, גנס האמין שהתחומים שתיאר עשויים לתווך בין נוצרים ליהודים בכך שישמשו נושא משותף ללימוד.
claims.quote: Gans believed that the disciplines he described might help to mediate between Christians and Jews, by serving as a shared subject of study.

claims.text: לפי אפרון, גנס רמז שאמונה זו בערך של המדעים לשיח בין-דתי הייתה משותפת גם לקפלר ולברהה.
claims.quote: his intimation that such beliefs were shared by Kepler and Brahé

claims.text: לפי הבלוג של הספרייה הלאומית, ב-1613, השנה שבה מת דוד גנס, עזב קפלר את פראג כדי להמשיך במחקרו.
claims.quote: In 1613, the same year that David Gans died, Kepler left Prague in order to further his research

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, החלק הראשון של הספר וקטעים מהשני תורגמו ללטינית בידי וילהלם היינריך פורסט (ליידן, 1644).
claims.quote: The first part of Gans's work, and extracts from the second, were translated into Latin by Wilhelm Heinrich Vorst (Leyden, 1644).

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, הספר תורגם גם ליידיש-גרמנית בידי שלמה האנאו (פרנקפורט, 1692).
claims.quote: It was translated also into Judæo-German by Solomon Hanau (Frankfort-on-the-Main, 1692).

claims.text: לפי הבלוג של הספרייה הלאומית, ספרו של גנס זמין היום לקריאה בעברית המקורית באתר הספרייה הלאומית של ישראל.
claims.quote: His book can now be read on the National Library of Israel website in the original Hebrew.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה היהודית, דברי הימים של גנס יבשים מאוד וללא ערך פנימי רב.
claims.quote: Though Gans's annals are very dry and have no great intrinsic value, they are memorable

claims.text: לפי כיכר השבת, היעב"ץ אסר ללמוד בקביעות את חלקו השני של "צמח דוד" שכתב גנס.
claims.quote: הספר השלישי אותו היעב"ץ אסר ללמוד בקביעות, הוא חלק ב' של ספר "צמח דוד", שכתב הרב דוד גנז

claims.text: לפי אפרון, תקוותיו של גנס לא התגשמו ורוב ספריו נותרו בלתי מפורסמים ומתעלמים מהם.
claims.quote: Gans's hopes went unfulfilled, and most of his books remained unpublished and ignored.

claims.text: לפי כיכר השבת, הרב גנס עבד לפרנסתו במצפה הכוכבים של האסטרונום טיכו ברהה יחד עם האסטרונום הגרמני יוהאנס קפלר.
claims.quote: הרב גנז, עבד לפרנסתו במצפה הכוכבים של האסטרונום הנודע 'טיכו ברהה' יחד עם האסטרונום הגרמני 'יוהאנס קפלר'.

claims.text: לפי ספריית לינדה הול, טיכו ברהה מת ב-24 באוקטובר 1601.
claims.quote: on Oct. 24, 1601, when Tycho died from uremia caused by a bladder problem

claims.text: לפי אוניברסיטת רוסטוק, מותו הפתאומי קטע את פרויקט לוחות מיקומי כוכבי הלכת שלו, ואת המלאכה השלים לבסוף קפלר.
claims.quote: It was Kepler who finally completed his master’s work.

quote_translations.c47: The second part of the book deals with the history of the nations of the world, and at its beginning Rabbi Gans apologizes for the compiled book
quote_translations.c50: Therefore Rabbi Gans emphasizes that he translated masses of gentile books dealing with history.
quote_translations.c49: After Rabbi Gans writes that there are sages who would rule not to read his book on Shabbat, he brings proof for his position from his teacher and master the Rema
quote_translations.c48: The third book that the Yaavetz forbade studying regularly is the second part of the book Tzemach David, written by Rabbi David Gans
quote_translations.c45: Rabbi Gans worked for his living at the observatory of the famed astronomer 'Tycho Brahe' together with the German astronomer 'Johannes Kepler'.
